This game is currently in the Humble Choice for January 2022.   If you are interested in the game and it's before February 1st, 2022, consider picking up the game as part of the current monthly bundle.

A keyboard-based hacking game.

Midnight Protocol calls itself a tactical RPG, though I disagree. Midnight Protocol is a strange keyboard-based game that completely removes the mouse from the game. It also is a hacking simulator where players have to breach networks that are more similar to Uplink or Hacknet. Though controlling the entire experience through just a command line makes for a very interesting experience. 

I’m a little shocked to announce this isn’t made by Zachtronics, and yet still really feels like a Zachtronics style game. The entire game gives the player the power to breach networks and then adds moral choices such as robbing random people and earning profits as a black hat hacker, or trying to remain noble as a white hat hacker. There’s a strong narrative as well, which is intriguing. 

Pick this up if you think you’d be willing to play a keyboard-based command-line game. The game is interesting and unique as you’ll see but if you aren’t intrigued by a game that only allows the player to use the keyboards, this one probably won’t be for you. It’s a special game, yet I adore this one. 

If you enjoyed this review or want to know what I think of other games in the bundle, check out the full review on or subscribe to my Youtube channel: https://youtu.be/j3gs3-4WiQI

review_text_raw:
Having played just about every hacking game under the sun, I played this less than two hours and I can clearly tell it's very promising. The keyboard-only interface is well crafted and refreshing. The initial missions have very clearly laid out tutorials that ease you into the various tools (and don't forget to type 'help *' if you should forget details).

Not being a fan of other time-based/stressful approaches, I greatly appreciate the developers' choice of going turn-based, making it all vastly more strategical. Here's to hoping this franchise will prosper, and a strong recommendation for all hacking game fans who may be turned off by annoying timers elsewhere.

review_text_raw:
[h1]Hack into a sci-fi near-future in an immersive, robust keyboard-only gameplay experience.[/h1]

Near-future science fiction is “set just far enough in the future to allow for certain technological or social changes without being so different that it is necessary to explain” ([i]Encyclopedia of Science Fiction[/i]). Taking place about 40 years in our future, [i]Midnight Protocol[/i] creates a remarkably robust and immersive gameplay experience using only keyboard commands - no mouse!

[h1]Game Universe[/h1]
Taking place in Budapest in the year 2062, the player takes on the persona of Data, a hacker arrested one year prior after being doxxed who has recently been released due to insufficient evidence. Along with their allies Clover (a hacker trained by Data) and Snail (an information broker), Data sets out to learn how their identity was uncovered and why it was exposed.

The story unfolds slowly, which makes sense for a game where the action is occurring within a computer universe. Much of the terminology will feel familiar to players knowledgeable about computers, such as command, program, SysOp, boot, and more. The subtle use of leetspeak and textspeak builds a realistic world without seeming overdone. For example, Clover’s nom de guerre is written as C10v3r for her username. There are also some interesting terminology choices, such as the word ‘deck’ for the programs selected to be taken on a particular mission.

[h1]Gameplay and Mechanics[/h1]
The Steam store describes [i]Midnight Protocol[/i] as “a tactical narrative-driven RPG”. The flavor of a particular playthrough is influenced by the player’s choices. Reputation can be gained in three areas that influence what missions and programs become available. Grey hat reputation will be required no matter what as it relates to Data’s accomplishments and skill as a hacker. White hat reputation relates to making choices favoring ideals, while black hat reputation relates to criminal or selfish actions. While I agree the game is narrative-driven, I feel the gameplay and mechanics have more in common with turn-based strategy games. There are broadly two areas of play: the home console and networks. 

The home console is where much of the story progression takes place, through email conversations and performing research on the intranet, as well as preparing for missions. The Port Scanner under Addresses can provide useful information about a network, such as what types of nodes will be present or the length of the trace bar. The player can only take a limited number of programs, called a deck, with them on each mission, so part of the strategy is deciding which programs to choose. For example, the player may want to take the leech program to help siphon funds from finance nodes or the spoon program to help decrypt encryption nodes. It reminds me of deck-building games, which is perhaps why the developers chose the term. As the game progresses, the player can choose to buy new programs or hardware from the Black Market, as long as they have sufficient credits, so it’s important to be choosy about which programs to buy in what order.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2634776057

Networks are where the turn-based aspect of the game comes into play. The player has 2 actions per turn, which include commands like moving to an adjacent node, running one of the programs from their deck, or interfacing with a node. There are different types of nodes (e.g., finance, encryption, bridge, data), and the interface command will be different at each type. For example, at an access node the interface command can be used to remove three traces from the Trace Bar once per mission. Most networks have some level of static protection in the form of Intrusion Countermeasure Electronics (ICE). Triggering an ICE will cause nasty effects for the player and increase the trace. The player passes the turn to the AI by using the end command. The network tries to trace the player on its turn, and if it succeeds enough times to max the Trace Bar it causes problems, such as loss of credits or deleted programs. Some networks will also have a Systems Operator (SysOp) that patrols the connections and adds an additional layer of strategy and challenge. Being cautious and checking a connection for ICE before moving takes time, but moving without checking runs the risk of triggering an ICE, so the player must balance speed and risk. Managing the distribution of processing slices per program is an essential part of gameplay strategy. Some programs require a set amount of slices and run a set number of turns, while some programs’ effectiveness depends on how many slices have been assigned to that program. Leaving slices idle at the end of a turn generally leads to less desirable outcomes. Once the objectives have been met, the player can use the exit command to leave the network. Unless otherwise stated, a mission cannot be replayed once it has been completed, so it is important to confirm that the desired outcome has been achieved before leaving the network.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2634776559

[h1]Art Style and Graphics[/h1]
The art style of [i]Midnight Protocol[/i] is minimalist, mainly using a monochromatic color scheme with purposeful noise reminiscent of analog television or VHS tapes. The home console user interface design is largely intuitive, and the player can choose from several themes to customize its appearance. All of the themes available at the start of the game are essentially monochromatic color schemes with varying levels of noise. There are additional themes that can be unlocked while playing, but I haven’t successfully done that yet in my playthroughs.

The visual representation of networks is where the game really shines. Different networks are visually distinct with consistent shapes for the node types. I found the default screen layout intuitive, but it is fully customizable if a player would prefer to change the location of components such as the Trace Bar or Objective List.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2634776907

[h1]Sound and Music[/h1]
The sound effects enhance the worldbuilding with typing as well as pinging, beeping, and other electronic elements on-brand for a hacker game, and the electronic aspects carry over into the music as well. The music of [i]Midnight Protocol[/i] is emotive yet subtle, “letting your keystrokes become part of the soundtrack” as the Steam store description says. As of the time of review, I haven’t encountered any voice acting in the game, but this makes sense considering the game’s immersive style. I’m interested to see if the music changes in the later game, particularly with regard to how the story evolves with white hat, grey hat, or black hat reputation.

[h1]Verdict[/h1]
[i]Midnight Protocol[/i] offers hours of content between the main plotline and optional side quests, as well as Steam trading cards and 18 possible achievements, making its $14.99 price tag (as of the time of review) more than fair. One flaw that merits a mention is the inability to save manually, which hampers full exploration of the different avenues without significant repetition. Since the game’s release the developers have been responsive to making improvements to the gameplay experience, so my fingers are crossed that manual saving becomes an option sometime in the future. I haven’t finished my initial playthrough yet, but I’m enjoying my time in the [i]Midnight Protocol[/i] universe. I would recommend [i]Midnight Protocol[/i] to fans of hacking games and culture, the near-future science fiction subgenre, or keyboard-only typing games.

review_text_raw:
[b]My Playtime:[/b] 29h (100% achievement, finished the game)
[b]Grindy Achievement(s):[/b] No.
[b]Optional Achievement(s):[/b] Yes (~9 achievements).
[b]Difficult Achievement(s):[/b] No.

[h1]Intro[/h1]
[b]Midnight Protocol[/b] is a simple turn-based strategy game with a hacking theme. You'll be able to explore nodes in a network and use programs to get data from them. The game offers multiple story branching, missions, and unlockables based on the path that you choose.

[b]Pros:[/b]
- Story branching depends on your choice in the mission
- 2 endings
- Those who don't like to read can still enjoy the game without doing so
- Various programs and hardware to use based on the mission and playstyle
- Difficulty can be changed anytime you want

[b]Cons:[/b]
- RNG-based, especially at the beginning of the game
- It can take a while to wait until the enemy finishes their turn
- Missions will be treated as finished if you exit the network
- Contrasting colors in some cutscenes (red on top of black/grey) can be problematic to some people

[b]Specs[/b]
Intel Core i5-9300H 2.40GHz, 8GB RAM, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650

[h1]Should you buy this game?[/h1]
[b]Yes.[/b]
[i]If you enjoy playing hacking games and don't mind playing one in a different genre, buy this game at a sale.[/i]

[hr][/hr]
[h1]In-Depth Review[/h1]

[h3]Visuals[/h3]
The visuals are divided into two parts: your computer and the network interface. The computer interface is more simplified, giving a lot of space to the text with switchable tabs. As for the network, they are depicted with a lot of interconnected nodes that you can travel to. To be honest, they don't look like a network at all, but the programs' visuals help to give that impression.

[h3]Story[/h3]
Dialogues in [b]Midnight Protocol[/b] are mostly about missions that you will take. A lot of events will happen at the same time as the main plot, which will get you involved in various things. I liked that they usually don't stop after one mission - it feels as if I was involved and making progress. As for the main plot, I found them to be alright. The presentation looks cool with the sudden contract of color, although some parts are still in mystery. The closure also feels realistic with everything going by as normal. However, despite the multiple endings, I don't think they differ that much to warrant another playthrough.

[h3]The Game[/h3]
[b]Gameplay[/b]
As I said before, the game is a turn-based strategy, albeit simplified. You'll have a series of interconnected nodes where you can travel and spawn programs to help you with your objectives. The objectives are varied in each mission, but basically, you need to explore all nodes and take out every object of interest, whether it's by downloading a file or routing money to your account. Some ICEs will guard some nodes in between, forcing you to spawn another program to take them out. Moreover, you need to do these while avoiding being traced, which will be randomized per turn based on your stealth capabilities.

Stealth is the most problematic aspect of this game. You only have a 75% chance not to be recognized enemy for each turn, and that's by using all of your slices, which is the equivalent of your system memory in-game. However, you will eventually need to summon more programs to do other things, which will require more slices. You can always lower the assigned slices in your stealth program, but doing so will lower its capabilities, making it easier for you to be traced by the enemy. I had to restart a mission several times in the beginning whenever the RNG screw me up and traced me every turn. It was boring to replay the missions and do the same thing again, hoping that the outcome will be different. The gear upgrades that were given after you play some missions help to overcome this, but you still need to tough it out before you got to that point.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2759479057

The early game is tough. Not only is the stealth mechanic isn't reliable, but the randomized enemies also can screw your run. You need to walk efficiently and not waste turns due to the RNG-based stealth, but enemies' locations are always hidden until you ran into them or used a sniffer program. Both options are not good either - the first option will increase your trace bar while the second one will eat 2 slices for 2 turns. It is easier to memorize enemies' locations before attempting your real run, but some enemies are placed randomly between more than one path. Again, this can be mitigated by purchasing upgrades after you reach a certain point.

The game gets better after you get enough upgrades. The RNG-based gameplay is still there, but it won't affect much to your experience. Moreover, numerous programs are available to help you build a deck that suits your playstyle. Since some missions are easier if you bring a certain program, you're bound to swap the programs from time to time.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2632524112

The reputation system can increase your difficulty. The game has a system that categorizes you into either white hat, grey hat, or black hat. This gives an impression that you can only choose one, although you can get as many reputations as you want in all categories. Some story-related missions might give a different reputation and outcome based on your action, but you never have to worry about anything apart from that. I refrained from taking anything that might increase my black hat reputation at first, which only penalize me from getting a benefit from that category and more money.

Money is limited at the early game. This might give issues to those who are trying to play the game purely as white hats since they are restricted from taking money from certain nodes. Moreover, those who quit the mission halfway will get penalized even more since the mission will be treated as completed without getting any reward. The game will give you a lot of money near the end of the game, but you won't need it at that point.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2759480074

[b]Length and Difficulty[/b]
The in-game clock says that I finished the game at 15:50:34, although [i]Steam[/i] said that I finished it in 26.6h. I had to retry some levels a few times to get a perfect result, and since you need to go to the main menu to buy more gears at the store in missions, it can take a while to load your save, especially with the unskippable animations. I spent the rest of my playtime figuring out the last achievement, which can be made shorter if you know what to do.

As for the difficulty, it can be hard at the beginning due to the RNG, but you can always change the difficulty in the options. I didn't change it apart from one mission, which I deemed impossible to finish at the normal difficulty due to the time limit. The final boss might also pose a problem if you choose to go on a certain route, although it is still doable by using certain programs.

[b]Problems[/b]
Some text can be hard to see due to the font color. Also, the in-game display can hinder you from seeing some information, such as the node address and how many turns you have left.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
[b]Midnight Protocol[/b] might be unpleasant to play at first due to the RNG, but it will soon be enjoyable once you have access to certain upgrades. My focus went to completing missions instead of the story, which is always unique in certain aspects. The game also offers more gameplay through the Workshop feature, although I soon got bored since I had to deal with the RNG again without my upgrades. Although I found some aspects to be lacking, I still could recommend [b]Midnight Protocol[/b] at a sale, provided that you are fine with the RNG-based gameplay.

As for the difficulty, it can be hard at the beginning due to the RNG, but you can always change the difficulty in the options. I didn't change it apart from one mission, which I deemed impossible to finish at the normal difficulty due to the time limit. The final boss might also pose a problem if you choose to go on a certain route, although it is still doable by using certain programs. [b]Problems[/b] Some text can be hard to see due to the font color. Also, the in-game display can hinder you from seeing some information, such as the node address and how many turns you have left. [h1]Conclusion[/h1] [b]Midnight Protocol[/b] might be unpleasant to play at first due to the RNG, but it will soon be enjoyable once you have access to certain upgrades. My focus went to completing missions instead of the story, which is always unique in certain aspects. The game also offers more gameplay through the Workshop feature, although I soon got bored since I had to deal with the RNG again without my upgrades. Although I found some aspects to be lacking, I still could recommend [b]Midnight Protocol[/b] at a sale, provided that you are fine with the RNG-based gameplay.

review_text_raw:
Midnight Protocol is rich in ambience, in intrigue, in tangled relationships of regret and camaraderie confidently conveyed in nothing more than text, and in more than its fair share of ingenuity.

It's also, unfortunately, like playing chess with only five pieces against a kid who can, at any time, go "yeah no but I had this super power set up HERE, right, all along I had this set up I did, and that means you can't get my guy and, uh, and, um, and and and WHOOOAAA EARTHQUAKE FLIPPED THE BOOOOARD"

You, master hacker that you are, are allowed to do two - count 'em - two succulent and juicy things per turn, and have to sulkily type out 'end' to end your turn thereafter. The goal is to make the most of limited resources against a seemingly unassailable adversary through deft moves and cunning. So far, so hacking-mentality - applaudable.

Yet the execution just doesn't quite make it. Effective red-teaming is about having recon good to go in advance against your target, which you never have in Midnight Protocol - and which costs you precious scant actions per turn to execute in the field instead. The jaws close on you all the while, unless you turn off the Trace mechanic altogether in the game options, and then you're just left with slowly hopping two-by-two across the board poking at things and slowly slurping up cash.

The plot is compelling, rich in injustices and laced with what-ifs, and I wanted to push through and see more of it. Unfortunately, there's a fair bit of padding in the early game that killed the momentum for me. I get it's good to establish characters, lay down rules and playstyles etc., but it'd be so much more exciting for these tidbits to come through organically while enjoying unravelling the story.

A shame, as there's a lot of cool-factor to the whole affair - it just isn't that fun to play.

Midnight Protocol is a desktop/hacking sim, and like all of these games, has nothing to do with actual hacking and is utterly unrealistic.  So this is just a strategy (turn based or realtime, you choose) game where you plug away controlling nodes or whatever.  The game does work but it's needlessly convoluted.  I guess to illustrate this, it takes 1/10th the time to learn how to play an RTS like Command & Conquer for 10x the rewarding gameplay.  And even though it's only a 2D game, C&C also has better graphics than this. 

The game design is somewhat flawed in some ways, with a reliance on procgen and RNG that can make or break each challenge. But mostly the game falls flat hard on a very weak and amateurish technical and visual presentation, and sloppy, and in some ways offensive interface design. 

On the upside, the game does feature customisable controls and resolution, so at least some of the basic, minimum requirements have been met.  Unfortunately there's a number of other technical defects and shortcomings which contribute to the game being difficult to recommend to gamers.

The game features lazy minimalist/untextured low-polygon "retro" assets and visuals, making this look like a barely functional 3D game from the early 1990s.  The lack of textures is a method that lazy devs often use to disguise their lack of talent/interest in doing the graphics properly and trying to disguise it under the name of "art", or "We made it look bad on purpose", which really isn't something gamers should have to put up with.  It's unclear why the developers weren't willing to arrange high quality, high polygon count contemporary assets and high resolution textures for the game.  It looks bad as a result of their decisions, and that's just another reason to avoid it.

To make matters worse, there's no mouse input, despite this being sold on PC as if it were a PC game.  This is unacceptable and somewhat insulting.  I know this is on purpose to make it seem like some kind of cool "hacker" game but this is annoying. Don't do this.  No developer should ever dictate to gamers how a game is to be played, ever. 

These technical defects push this game below acceptable standards for any modern PC game.

Midnight Protocol didn't appeal much to the people who own a copy of the game, either.  It has achievements, and they show us a very clear picture that the game didn't really capture any interest from gamers.  The most commonly and easily attained achievement is for finishing the tutorial, trivial to get, but less than 39 percent of players bothered to get that far before uninstalling the game.  Hardly a success story, gamers just weren't all that interested in the game.

So, should you buy this game?  Is this one of the best of the 100,000+ games on Steam?

Midnight Protocol has the laughable, eye-watering price of $15 USD, for which you could easily get any number of older AAA games.  Given the defects and quality issues with the game, coupled with the unrealistic price, this is impossible to recommend.

For comparison, the $15 asking price for this game could get you games like "Mass Effect Andromeda", "Project Zomboid" or "Stellaris".  Quality, professionally made games like those are frequently on sale cheaper than this.

[url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/beatnuki/recommended/1162700/]I pretty much gotta agree with this review[/url].

The developers advertised it on Netrunner adjacent boards. Unfortunately, that's as far as the Netrunner elements go.

You're playing a computer hacker (aka: "Runner" which isn't the term here, so not Netrunner releated) breaking into systems to figure out what has gone on since you were released from jail. Mayhem and hacking ensues.

But the thing is: For all the talk about being Netrunner inspired... it doesn't work. Both you and the AI/SysOp have two actions a turn (compared to Netrunners' 4 Runner 3 SysOp actions a turn). This would be fine... [b][i]IF[/i] the gameplay wasn't timed with the "trace" mechanic[/b] (unlike Netrunners, you can't remove it and you can't buy over the SysOp/Corp to bounce it/avoid the trace).

So you're racing against the clock, facecheck (slam into an ICE defense) and... get fucked over massively in terms of the timer/trace raising in addition to losing an action to where you can't course correct same turn. This means you'll get "trace++" 2+ traces in addition to the end turn trace (which if some ICE is hit, turns off your "cloak" function to try to prevent/stop the trace from increasing, say HELLO to 2-3+ traces off a faceslam).

[i]This is where the game becomes unfun[/i] and if I didn't run into the above review, I would've quit instead of finding the "turn the trace mechanic off" and as the review states: That makes the game somewhat boring because you're [i]turning off an anxiety/timer mechanic[/i] but after a certain point you're like "ok, I'm screwed five ways, why have a sixth?"

Interesting story to go through, but honestly: No, not worth the money. Check the demo out, if you're able to put up with the bad design (needed some more passes to be a bit more fair on the players), go for it. But honestly? I can't recommend it.

Hopefully NetSpectre gives me the Netrunner-a-like I want, but I'm kind of doubting it.

Slay the Spire is pretty much the only one that comes close and even THAT isn't going for Netrunner, but took elements from it.

...My search continues...

review_text_raw:
I cautiously recommend this game. It's great on the whole, but there were a couple design choices which [b]really[/b] bugged me and nearly caused me to give a thumbs down. Those two things were: [b]the usage of RNG & the game's subsequent reliance on rollbacks (do-overs).[/b]

I'm a huge fan of hacking games. They are one of my favorite niche-genres of games. Generally speaking, the gameplay in a hacking game follows a simple formula: poke at a "server" and strip its defenses using various tools until it can be "connected to." This is often done with a time limit.

Midnight Protocol challenges this formula by translating the process into a turn based affair. In many ways, it plays like a turn based RPG. On a conceptual level, this is a cool idea. I was excited when I read about it. In practice, however, I found that it [strike]encouraged[/strike] [b]mandated[/b] save scumming. I mean this as constructively as possible - [b]I hate this.[/b]

I'll elaborate:

When I was forced to repeat a mission in [b][i]Hacknet[/i][/b], it was because I wasn't fast enough. The onus was on [b]ME[/b] to improve my skills. I needed to be faster. I had all the tools, but I came up short.

When I was forced to repeat a mission in [b][i]Midnight Protocol[/i][/b], it was because [b]the game's RNG[/b] dealt me an [i]objectively unwinnable[/i] scenario. The SysOp wandered into my node, or the "random" trace mechanic in Pavo's mission installed a Sundrop 10 nodes away.

This isn't interesting or engaging gameplay. I'm not learning anything, and I'm not becoming a better player. I'm just waiting for a luckier break.

Now, it would be one thing if you could "embrace failure" like you can in a game like XCOM or Rimworld - but you can't in Midnight Protocol. Most key missions actually prevent you from disconnecting until you complete your main objective. You are expected to rollback if you fail.

[i]My next two particular criticisms were addressed in a patch on 10/18/21. Respect.[/i]

[strike]RNG isn't the only thing causing me to rollback missions. The game gives you a peek at what kind of nodes & defenses you will be up against, allowing you to choose the appropriate programs for the job. For rank & file side-missions, this generally isn't a big deal. But for some of the larger story missions, you need fairly specific loadouts to have a fighting chance. It's not uncommon for me to get 8+ turns into a mission before I find myself thinking "Yeah I can't do this without Tunnel" and rolling back.

But it gets a little worse - ICE can be hidden... [i]and its location in missions is static.[/i] This means that after I (am forced to) rollback, I now know where the ICE is, and the mission is partially spoiled. It's up to me if I want to "pretend" not to know that.[/strike]

I've spent a lot of real estate here ragging on the RNG/Rollback mechanics, but I want to reiterate that I still recommend this game.

When the RNG gods [i]aren't[/i] busy strangling me, I actually really enjoy the turn based gameplay. It's a welcome twist on the genre that makes it feel truly different. The presentation is phenomenal (would have liked some more lively music though). And I really like the open ended narrative allowing you to chase leads & reply to emails. Simulation is an important part of hacking games, and I love the agency that the game gives us.

Well polished hacking games are an extreme rarity. There's been like... 5 since Uplink came out in 2001. I'm happy this game exists and I'm enjoying my time with it on the whole. I just wish RNG wasn't so strongly relied upon in its design.

The presentation is phenomenal (would have liked some more lively music though). And I really like the open ended narrative allowing you to chase leads & reply to emails. Simulation is an important part of hacking games, and I love the agency that the game gives us. Well polished hacking games are an extreme rarity. There's been like... 5 since Uplink came out in 2001. I'm happy this game exists and I'm enjoying my time with it on the whole. I just wish RNG wasn't so strongly relied upon in its design.

Midnight Protocol, developed by LuGus Studios and published by Iceberg Interactive, is a masterfully constructed cyberpunk hacking RPG that forgoes the flashy aesthetics of most games in its genre in favor of tension, intellect, and immersion. It tells the story of a hacker known as Data, who is drawn back into the digital underworld after being doxxed and exposed. The narrative unfolds through encrypted emails, terse chat messages, and system logs, building a world of espionage, distrust, and digital warfare without ever showing a single human face. The game’s story is deeply personal, portraying the isolation and moral grayness of living behind the screen, where every keystroke carries risk and consequence. What begins as a simple act of self-defense quickly evolves into a web of political intrigue, corporate corruption, and cyber rebellion, all told through the restrained, text-based aesthetic of a command-line interface.

The most striking element of Midnight Protocol is its complete commitment to its design philosophy. Every action is performed through the keyboard—no mouse, no icons, just commands typed into a digital terminal. This approach is not merely a stylistic choice but a fundamental part of the experience. It places the player directly in the mindset of a hacker, forcing you to think in terms of efficiency, logic, and spatial reasoning. Networks are depicted as interconnected nodes, each representing firewalls, data caches, security systems, or hidden traps. Your goal varies from mission to mission: infiltrate corporate systems, extract sensitive data, disable rival programs, or manipulate information to your advantage. Each network functions as a puzzle, requiring you to manage limited resources, stay ahead of traces, and decide how far you can push before the system locks you out. Every move carries tension, and the thrill of narrowly escaping detection provides a constant pulse of adrenaline.

What makes these mechanics so engrossing is how they combine strategic planning with improvisation. Each mission feels like a high-stakes chess match played against invisible opponents. You have a library of programs at your disposal—some for stealth, others for brute-force attacks—and choosing the right combination is crucial. The trace system, which measures how close the authorities are to locating you, ensures that every decision feels urgent. Some players might find the reliance on randomness in the trace and detection mechanics slightly frustrating, as even well-planned strategies can fall apart under bad luck. Yet, this unpredictability mirrors the nature of hacking itself—controlled chaos within an unstable system. As your reputation grows and your alignment shifts between white-hat idealism, gray-hat pragmatism, and black-hat ruthlessness, the missions, tools, and story outcomes evolve to reflect your choices. This morality system adds replayability and depth, as it allows players to craft a hacker identity that aligns with their philosophy.

The game’s progression system is intricately tied to its tone of calculated mastery. Through black markets and secret contacts, you acquire new software, upgrade existing tools, and refine your build into a precise digital arsenal. Different playstyles emerge naturally—one player may rely on stealth programs to bypass ICE unnoticed, while another might embrace aggressive, virus-based attacks to dismantle defenses entirely. The learning curve is smooth but demanding, gradually pushing players toward mastery without resorting to handholding. It’s the kind of game that rewards patience and experimentation; every failure is a lesson in systems thinking. The world expands organically through your own initiative: new missions arrive via encrypted emails, hidden coordinates, or anonymous requests. Even the mundane act of checking your in-game inbox feels immersive, as if you are living within a network of digital conspiracies.

Visually, Midnight Protocol is minimalist yet elegant. The interface is clean, the color palette subdued but purposeful—shades of neon blue, black, and red evoke the cold pulse of cyberspace. Despite its simplicity, the design feels immersive, capturing the essence of a digital battlefield through pure abstraction. Every flicker of light and distortion effect contributes to the illusion that you are operating from the edge of legality. The sound design amplifies this immersion with sharp beeps, data pulses, and the low hum of electronic machinery that underscore each command you enter. There is no voice acting or cinematic interlude, but this absence enhances the sense of isolation and authenticity. You are a ghost in the network, unseen and unheard, communicating only through code and action.

The pacing of Midnight Protocol is deliberate, structured around cycles of tension and relief. Missions can be completed in short bursts, yet each one feels meaningful. There are no filler objectives; everything you do contributes to the unraveling of the narrative or your personal evolution as a hacker. While the game never overstays its welcome, some players may wish for a broader scope or more diverse mission environments. The story’s intimate scale, however, fits the tone—this is not about saving the world but about surviving it, carving your path through the static and deceit of a system that’s stacked against you. The writing is terse and precise, and though the characters are only ever seen through text, they feel real, shaped by ideology and consequence rather than cliché.

Midnight Protocol succeeds because it understands exactly what it wants to be—a cerebral, atmospheric strategy game that thrives on immersion, tension, and mechanical purity. It captures the loneliness and allure of the digital frontier, where information is power and morality is fluid. Its stripped-down design and keyboard-driven gameplay make it a niche experience, but within that niche lies something exceptional: a game that makes you feel like a real hacker, navigating systems not through spectacle, but through intellect. It’s a rare experience that balances narrative intrigue with strategic complexity, one that demands attention and rewards mastery. For those who crave precision, immersion, and the thrill of the unknown, Midnight Protocol is a digital labyrinth worth exploring line by line, command by command.

An interesting concept. With all the interesting programs you can add to your deck, this should have been a solid turn-based strategy/puzzle game, but it's so restrictive and RNG-based from the start that it can easily turn into a "try, die, repeat until you get lucky" experience. After my sixth time restarting a single mission because of bad luck rather than lack of skill (getting a trace+ three times in a row despite having cloak at 75%, SysOps making a beeline for me at exactly the wrong moment, etc.), I realized I wasn't having fun anymore, so I turned it off and sorted it into my "not worth it" pile.

It's a shame, because there was a lot of potential to love here and it would have been right up my alley if the RNG was a little more forgiving.

EDIT: Devs have pointed out that there ARE difficulty settings. It took me a bit to find them, but they do exist, so I've edited the review to reflect that and to add examples for the bad luck I had.

I was having a great time until the "SysOp" gameplay showed up. I didn't understand what other reviewers meant by "like Chess" until then. This isn't really a puzzle or hacking game like I thought it was, it's a board game. That should be in giant letters at the top of the store listing. BOARD GAME. It's not about solving the map, it's about outplaying an AI. You are essentially moving your queen around the board to different squares while trying to avoid opposing pieces that are coming for your piece. This system shows up 6 hours in, after you've already spent your time with the game as a puzzle game, without the "SysOp" stuff. That was an extremely engaging me\ntal exercise in figuring out how to beat the level. The SysOp now becomes how to beat an opponent, and that is less compelling to me as a game. Unfortunately this game altering mechanism doesnt show up until well after the refund period.

Make crystal clear you want to play a CHESS style board game before you buy this. It's well made and polished, but it's not a puzzle or mystery or "hacking" game. Ultimately it isn't for me, and I'm bummed it's not closer to what the store listing makes it out to be. I think if the developer had better set expectations going in I would have a better impression.

review_text_raw:
[h1] You are chaos embodied. [/h1]
Unhinged. Untested. Unstoppable. The keyboard is a natural extension of you. An arm, a tendril with which you tap into a vast, deep, unknowable ocean. 
And you believe the proper, nay, the only way to play chess is with a game clock. 
Act before you think. If you fail, try again. 
Run wild. Run blind. 

I do recommend that anyone interested in a keyboard/console based game give Midnight Protocol a shot. The RTS mode is an experience to be had. Besides, the demo is free, and I'm pretty sure you can already try that mode in there?

DISCLAIMER: This review is written for the RTS variant of gameplay. I have only played a bit past tutorial with its turn-based mode so there would be a bit of speculation on that portion of gameplay. 

I think the game truly had something unique, behind its "not recommended" way to play. It just feels so paradoxical: on one hand, I can't imagine them having developed this mode later, with so many of the game's elements seemingly originating from a more time-based perspective (for example, the money drain being continuous when you got fully-traced, or the final trace countdown in general). It also just feels impossible that someone would make a "hacking" game that doesn't reward lightning fast fingers and an innate familiarity with the console. On the other, so many of the "transplanted" features feel forced, imbalanced, as if the devs spent little effort trying to make the RTS mode actually enjoyable overall, among them the top culprits being oft-misleading card texts, or multiple challenges requiring interactions with the trace meter that is impossible to do in RTS, making them impossible to complete, or worse, Onion being a card that exists which completely trivializes the Trace Meter in RTS mode, and Hive being completely nuts that there's next to no reason to use any other breaker except for a select few situations. Perchance. 

I don't think any other game quite captures that chaotic energy as well as Midnight Protocol did for its first few missions. The scramble to get objectives done, timing drains just in time to avoid getting hit by its cooldown, juggling sniffers and dashing back and forth to sniff the next connection on an ice-ridden network... 
Quite unfortunately, the game trying to make itself a turn-based thing really runs at odds with its hacker-esque aesthetic. So many opportunities lost just to make it a middling strategy game with a mediocre story. That decision may have come from a genuine place of good intentions, perhaps to make it accessible to those not well-versed with a keyboard, or those who would much prefer the more methodical approach. Without a timer breathing down your neck, demanding you to act now, I don't think the Poison debuffs, or being backed into a corner by various bosses, would feel nearly as intense. The first time I ran through the first Wire Trial was most certainly heart-attack inducing. I ran blind. I ran wild. And miserable was my failure. Perchance. 

I don't know where this game belongs. It looks, feels and plays extremely polished and smooth, yet its mechanics, its progression/difficulty curve, and its -- quite frankly -- odd karma system adds very little to gameplay or story. It's as if a master of design did the moment-to-moment gameplay, a professional artist did the paintjob, then a monkey did everything in between. Perchance.

review_text_raw:
You know, I almost think that the Indiepocalypse was a good thing. Before, you could release a pretty mediocre, unpolished experience and you'd still sell a bunch of copies. Now devs are scrambling to have absolutely all elements of the game adjusted to perfection... and have only 116 reviews on Steam. So there's a bunch of sublime, absolutely excellent titles on Steam which nobody plays, and the dev's life is ruined. Ok, that's not very nice actually.

Midnight Protocol is one of those games. It manages to reproduce the *feeling* of hacking while making the gameplay incredibly engaging, and tells a gripping, morally challenging story about the future of the internet and the reality of hacktivism. Just beware: this game is played using keyboard only, by typing commands. No time pressure, tho.

To explain the gameplay a bit more: it's nothing like other hacking games like Uplink; in fact it's unlike anything, full stop. It's a tactical turn-based "network crawler" in which you constantly try to avoid getting traced while trying to complete the mission objective (usually activate some node, or steal money, or download a piece of data). 

You'll have to deal with firewalls (ICEs), SysOps, and the unrelenting trace protocol which ticks every turn. And you're never 100% safe from it; it will get you eventually. But if you rush too much, you might run into firewalls, or alert the SysOp to your presence. So it becomes a constantly changing game of resource and risk management.

And the stakes are high. There are some routine, insignificant missions, yes. But the majority ask interesting questions about morality of technology, ask you to consider your principles, and some are literally about someone's life and death... and perhaps even more. That, combined with the ever ticking trace protocol, drive the tension through the roof - your brain is always at 100% processing while playing this; never a dull moment.

Of course, you're given a set of tools to accomplish your goals. Your deck - programs you bring with you on a mission, as well as your hardware - passive bonuses. As you progress, you unlock new pieces, which often you also have to buy, and money's tight early on. And while the hardware gives you a clear advantage, the new programs aren't necessarily better; everything comes with a cost. And it's up to you to construct a deck which minimises the cost but maximises the advantage, all while keeping an eye on what is best for this particular mission.

Of particular note is the music in this game. It breaks seemingly all rules of sensible design by having essentially two tracks playing for the majority of the game. One for "normal" missions, and one for more important ones. In the latter, as the trace bar slowly but surely fills, the music is becoming more and more intense. This takes the already sky-high feeling of tension and launches it into the outer orbit.

To wrap things up, writing. It's way better than I thought it would be. The story is coherent, has constant twists and turns, keeps you in its grip, and makes excellent usage of the Chekhov's Gun. It's also unique because it's a hacking story that takes place in the EU in the 2060s - and it's a very believable representation. Your character resides in Budapest, but other European cities also make an appearance, such as Berlin with it's tech hub. 

If you're wondering why I only wrote good things, it's because I can't really think of anything bad. And my standards are high. If anything, I'm very displeased that the game has only 116 reviews at the time of writing, indicating it didn't sell very well; I'm hoping I convinced you to help fix that problem a little. Enjoy!

And this is about it when it comes to the positives.

It's almost fundamentally not a hacking game. You could easily swap out all of the "commands" for just fantasy spells. You're not breaking into systems to gather information, to gather passwords to use on other networks (i.e. puzzle solving). Each "mission" is fundamentally independent. You're there to get money (or complete objectives for the story) and then leave.

The developer has a solid foundation to creating an interesting hacking game. But if they're going to do a RNG/RPG turn-based game, then stick to fantasy/sci-fi instead.

Hacking games are among my favorites. Making one into a sort of hybrid RPG and turn-based strategy game was a good idea, and the execution is solid. I have a pretty low frustration threshold for games - I play everything on easy mode if it's available - but despite that and the fact I don't have much experience with strategy games, this one didn't ever make me angry. I will say the difficulty curve feels a bit awkward, as I found the most challenging mission by far to be one that happens before you head into the climax. It's followed by several really easy ones, and the final boss fight was also surprisingly quick and easy. Not a big complaint, but something to be aware of.

I liked the visual style of the game, with the sparse "digital game board" and its glowing TRON-ish aesthetic, the Hollywood Hacking style console readouts, error messages and the like, the single-color wireframe models for enemies and traps, and the pleasing, sleek UI of the terminal you use between missions. The music was also great and fit the theme perfectly. The keyboard-only controls were easy to pick up, and since the game doesn't require quick inputs or reflexes, they don't hinder playability.

The RPG elements were a bit hit-or-miss for me - a lot of the available upgrades or programs seemed fairly worthless, and I settled into ones I liked and stuck with them for the most part. Sometimes you will need a specific tool for a certain mission, and thankfully the game lets you restart any mission and change your loadout at any point. While some elements of the gameplay are randomized, things like trap placement and passwords you need to know aren't, so even if you fail a mission you usually learn something useful to remember on your next attempt. There is definitely some trial and error necessary, but it wasn't enough to bother me.

The game does offer a branching storyline, and it keeps track of and displays relevant decisions, but it wasn't always clear to me that I actually had a choice. I liked it enough that I'll probably try replaying it to make different choices and see some of the content I missed, but it was a little disappointing on occasion to feel like I was railroaded into doing something when I apparently could have gone a different route.

The plot is fine, but nothing particularly original or special. If you've played sci-fi hacking games before you're going to notice a lot of similar or recycled story elements, and none of the twists really surprised me. I didn't have the same sense of high stakes or tough moral decisions that I had in Hacknet, for example. Still, it was decently interesting as a complement to the gameplay.

If this seems like the sort of thing you might be interested in, I definitely recommend giving it a go. It's a well-put-together title in this little subgenre that may be a bit samey in narrative and visuals but offers a different and interesting take on the gameplay concepts.

The game gently makes you understand that the ever-expanding arsenal of tools is not a soulless inventory clutter, but an expansion of your capabilities, which is not always immediately clear, but requires training. For this, there is also a training ground, where without any risk you can try out some new tactics, study the weak and strong points of your tools. Really enjoyed this, both the puzzles and the story and the hacking aesthetic. Fundamentally, the elevator pitch of this game is "Mankind Divided if it was collapsed to its hacking mini-game (but turn-based)". If you are a fan of turn-based tactics and H A C K I N G (or sci-fi in general), then I would strongly recommend this game.

+ The puzzle/tactics aspect is fun and varied. You continuously gain new abilities, but they complement, rather than replace, the ones you already have.
+ The missions are quite diverse and varied too, requiring you to shuffle your build from mission to mission.
+ The story is a very solid sci-fi tale with a decent amount of world-building and side-quests. So even though the main quest is always flashing on your screen, you can get at least somewhat immersed in the world and its history on the side, which I greatly appreciate.
+ There is a fair bit of non-linearity, with the intent being that "any choice you make is valid", which lends a lot of credibility to the narrative, and makes the choices you make that much more meaningful (as opposed to "do you accept a generic sidequest? y/n"). At least early on.

- My main complaint would probably be about the slight schizophrenia in game/mission design that the game succumbs to. On the one hand, the game suggests that "any choice is valid", meaning the player is expected to roll with the punches -- you should prepare for any mission the best you can based on the info given to you in advance, and any mission you fail weighs on your consciousness, but the story continues regardless. (For the record, I tried my best to adhere to this philosophy and accept the consequences.) However, about half-way through, the game starts saying "hey, this mission is critical, you can't quit and you can't fail", so if you fail you just start over (with an option to change your loadout). In effect, this means that in most missions from that point onwards, you have no choice but to savescum: first see the mission, learn the layout and the threats, and then equip the optimal loadout. 
I understand the difficulties of mission design and narrative design and all kinds of design that led to this outcome, but as a player, at that point I felt cheated. As a "reviewer", I am not sure what could have been a better way. Leaning all-in on the "everything allowed" approach would've put a very low difficulty ceiling and/or required a *lot* of extra writing. Taking it out completely would greatly harm the immersion the game offers in the first half. So... yeah... It's good but I can't help but wonder if it could've been even better.

- Also 0451 doesn't open any doors, bad cyberpunk game, 2/10. (Or does it? This playthrough took too long...)

I'm always on the hunt for good hacking games on Steam, so when I saw Midnight Protocol, I just had to get it.
Turn based games usually put me off, however the devs really ironed this mechanic out and it gives you a good amount of breathing room to plan out your next steps. 

Having played Uplink (With Uplink OS), Hacknet, Grey Hack and Hackmud, I felt right at home with this game. Granted, it doesn't try to be what Grey Hack or Hackmud are (especially due to the lack of multiplayer) but I gotta say it really captures the classic atmosphere of Uplink and the vibe of Hacknet.

I highly recommend this game.

I got this from Humble Bundle's Humble Choice January 2022. I've played Hacknet (another great hacking game) and thought this would be similar based off the screenshots. The only similarities is that they are both hacking themed, and you could type commands.

[h1] Playthrough [/h1]
Midnight Protocol took me almost 30hours to 100%, which was done in two playthroughs. The main story is the same but choices in the side quests do affect how much more side quests (and achievements) to play through. Playing through more missions helps give you more credits to buy more programs and also to rank up your Hat reputation to unlock new programs and hardware. Missing out on reputation ranks does not seem to affect the main story, but it seems that the main story will not progress until you resolve the side quests (by finishing or rejecting them)

[h1] Gameplay [/h1]
Midnight protocol plays more like a turn based board game with puzzles. You have two actions to move around the map, solve puzzles, break ICE (firewalls and traps), and maybe steal some money [strike] (I stole from a dead person's savings account saving up for their mom) [/strike], all while trying to complete the mission objectives. After every turn, the trace protocol will roll their dice and determine how much longer you can stay on the map until the trace bar completes. In later maps, there might be SysOps who will try to protect their network to try and stop you.

The turn based mechanic allows players to choose to play either fast and dangerous by rushing the objectives but might raise the trace quicker, or slow and stealthily by cloaking from the trace and slowly destroying hindrances but safely (better chance trace might not increase). Personally, I enjoy going through every nook and cranny so I take my time slowly stealthily going through the maps (didn't take Mask off most missions, even sysops). In my second playthrough, I found it wasn't all that necessary to play so slowly since most missions actually have enough trace bar to play quicker and more aggressively.

[h1] Story [/h1]
I thought the main story and even all the side stories were great. Side stories help build up the world, giving more information on the different organizations and how the world is. It also foreshadows themes really well back into the main story. Some side stories that aren't directly involved with the main story or the world, but these feel like easter eggs that reward players who enjoy looking through everything.

review_text_raw:
Let me start off by saying that this game is way better than Uplink. (Despite being somewhat inspired by it)

Midnight Protocol is a turn-based strategy game with some RPG elements. The game is 100% played on your keyboard and you type the commands that you want to perform while moving around a board. Commands range from offensive or stealth, with a multitude of types to choose from and while navigating the board, you are destroying/avoiding antivirus programs called ICE as well as security system admins called Sys ops. While it might not sound like much at first,  the gameplay is a solid, intense and addictive experience.

The story and characters in Midnight Protocol are enthralling, and kept me constantly guessing as to what was going to happen next. To be brief, you are a reputable hacker named DATA taking on jobs for people from all walks of life. Your jobs range from hacking into banks, planting evidence, and deleting evidence of infidelity off of some couples' iCloud to prevent some idiot's divorce. (No, seriously.) 

One thing that this game handles very well, in my opinion, is choice. In almost every mission, you are given a choice that affects your moral standing in the game' s world. The game measures your choices and you have 3 meters: White hat (Good), Black hat (Bad), Gray hat (Morally grey). A nice touch considering that hackers in this world (as well as somewhat in our own) are considered to be modern day outlaws. A good chunk of your choices are meaningful for the ending, and almost none are easy which I think is where this game really shines.

To get into negatives, there is a warning when you open the game that tells you that the game is controlled solely through the keyboard. That's completely understandable the first time you launch the game, but not every time. There’s also no way to turn this off for some reason to my knowledge and it became pretty annoying after launching the game for the first time. Another negative I wanted to mention is that there is a MAJOR difficulty spike towards the end of the game. Having things get harder towards the end of a game makes absolute sense, but it felt like the game’s difficulty curve went from an incline to a straight up 90 degree angle. 

To conclude, I wanted to leave this great game a review seeing as how it doesn’t have enough of them and definitely deserves a bit more love.

4/5

review_text_raw:
When people talk about the power of indie video games, they mean games like this one. A tight turn-based strategy game underpins a well-written story with a branching narrative and compelling characters. The overall length of the game at 20 hours was, for me, absolutely perfect. This is a rare game where I picked it up on a discount and find myself angry I didn't pay more for the experience.

The game itself is about you, a hacker returning from a year of incarceration with a need to know what sent you there. Along the way, you breech systems in a turn-based strategy game similar to Invisible, Inc. Whereas in that game you play physical agents, in this one you play a digital representation ripped straight out of cyberpunk fiction like Neuromancer. Customize your deck with new chips so you can slot more programs and be prepared for some visual surprises - while the game plays true to form with the genre, it manages to break expectations any time the game begins to feel stale.

My biggest complaints (and they are fairly minor) are around the customizations. I felt like the deck you have has just a few too few viable options or that some choices didn't really seem plausible. For instance, you have the expected upgrades, such as more "slices" to run more programs at once, or memory capacity to slot more programs into your deck, but you also have a bunch of upgrades which feel pretty pointless. I tried one that was supposed to give you more credits (trailing a crimson thread behind you and incentivizing exploring a network more deeply) but the core upgrades are so important, there's not room for fanciful choices such as these. That said, there are actually enough choices that I did have to rearrange both my hardware and software to overcome levels, and that felt like I was making smart choices.

I will have to find time for another play-through now that I have a better sense of the story, and so I can capture all the easter eggs buried in this passion project. I hope someday we get a Midnight Protocol 2 in the same universe, though perhaps with different characters. And to the creators, thank you for bringing this story to life.

review_text_raw:
This is a game that while via screenshots, doesn't look like much, is a very very cool unique take on the "hacking" genre.  It's entirely keyboard driven, and while that may feel like a hindrance, it actually adds to the game's immersion.  All controls are well thought out and seamless, and there's no awkward switching between mouse and keyboard like many typical games might do.

The gameplay itself is a little bit puzzle and a healthy dose of turn based tactics.  There's some RNG involved, and while you can't save scum individual moves, restarting a level is quick and painless, so if you really get boned by RNG (rare but could happen), you don't feel bad giving it another shot.

Honestly, it feels like XCOM in how it feels to do well (or poorly), getting a few lucky dice rolls, or missing a few 90% shots, but there's usually enough wiggle room baked in that it doesn't ruin your run.

There's also a cool RPG-ish element of progression.  As you get further, you buy new programs and hardware to customize your abilities.  Do you want to be stealthy and slow?  Do you want to be fast and brash?  Do you need a sniper program to deal with a long range enemy, or one that helps you open additional paths from a distance to skirt a danger?

On top of all that, the presentation is much slicker in game than screenshots may reveal.  Everything is cohesive in feel, animated in a flashy, but appropriate manner.  The sound effects and music are very hacker feeling and enjoyable. 

Finally, there's actually a story!  I'm still going through it, so I can't comment on its entire arc, but it involves you working with friends to accomplish various goals, and there's a range of personal crisis, professional concerns, morality.  It actually feels somewhat real, like you're actually emailing other people, and it adds some reasons to what you're doing.

All in all, an unusual game that's well worth playing.

Midnight Protocol is a fun, surprisingly expansive hacking game that does an excellent job of balancing tension and difficulty with flexible gameplay and a deep, thoughtful story. This isn't a real-time hacking sim like Uplink or Nethack -- it's a turn-based, more puzzle-oriented game where you're exploring systems while dodging ICE and enemy operators (though like those games, it's controlled 100% by typing). But make no mistake, even with its turn-based nature it still manages to ratchet up the tension as trace meters rise and turn timers tick down.

What I enjoyed was that the wide variety of apps and hardware systems let players approach security systems in multiple ways. For instance, my go-to kit was a slow and steady loadout of high trace security and the "hive" program which grows in power for each infected system node. I would methodically march around systems, infecting everywhere I touched while staying under the radar, until I could hammer away at the ICE security systems with a powerful strike. Thankfully, though, the game forces you to adapt by mixing up security systems and other gameplay elements. I had to toss my approach out the window for levels that had strict turn timers, ditching security for a deck geared around an all-out hacking sprint.

The story is excellent and surprised me with its depth and complexity, including multiple opportunities for player choice and expression. Almost every conversation is strictly via email or chat but by the end the game had crafted multiple fully fleshed-out characters who I was deeply invested in.

I wish more people would play this game. If you're a fan of hacking games, puzzlers, or board games (the gameplay elements seem wonderfully suited for a tabletop edition), I highly recommend it.

An enjoyable investigative puzzle game, Midnight Protocol has good writing, reinforced by clever changes in the UI and the visual respresentation of dataspace with every level. The game succeeds in creating the appropriate mood when it needs to, with music that alters alongside the tension, or meta elements involving a desktop crash or UI corruption. Some of the puzzles require innovative thinking, or a re-examination of what is at your disposal, which makes it rewarding to find a solution.

The strategic part comes through the deck and hardware customisation, which is well-tied into the story and gameplay. Optional challenges for extra credits encourage change; combined with mission-required programs and the natural slot limit, it encourages you to think and change your plan as required. I found the 'rollback' command, allowing the player to retry the mission with a different loadout, to be an essential part of adapting an approach, as the tactics to complete an actual level is tied heavily into your loadout choices. No prior knowledge of programming is required to play, and the game provides in-level help for any command the player needs.

The percentage chance for trace progression, which leads to a level's failure condition, is something that might appear frustrating if the player has few options (such as near the beginning of the game with limited programs available), but no level is impossible, and as a turn-based game with unlimited retries, there is plenty of time to think and plan, which makes the eventual success more satisfying.

At face value I was uncertain, but after twenty-eight hours of playtime and playing nothing else until I finished it, I am certain that Midnight Protocol is a good game that could be worth your attention.

Its gameplay doesn't have much to do with real-life hacking but it will make you feel like a hacker.
It's a collection of tactical minigames in which you move through abstract networks avoiding or eliminating obstacles and collecting resources. That's basically it. Comparing Midnight Protocol to Hacknet doesn't make much sense because the games are so different mechanically.

In addition to solid tactical puzzles that get more complex as the game progresses, there's a strong narrative wtih rpg elements - you choose to be a good or a bad guy and the story adapts. It would take at least 2 playthroughs to see all the content (one playtrough took me 21 hrs including all side missions in turn-based mode). Visuals are top notch, minimalistic and elegant. (However, I miss the ability to rotate the view like in Invisible Inc.). The atmosphere of the operating system combined with typing commands really made me feel like I was playing the part of a hacker. The emails received make the game feel surprisingly lifelike for the amount of text the game is made of. The choices I made allowed me to unlock different upgrades, and at times I was making decisions I didn't necessarily agree with just so I could get an unlock, which certainly made me feel some type of way. At times I found myself examining the gray area in actions which were considered selfish. It's okay to steal from this lady's personal savings for this reason but not from her daughter's college fund, so I'll leave that alone. 

I spent around 20-25 hours completing the story, all side missions, and 66% of achievements. I would definitely recommend picking it up if you like tactical games. The game at full price is a steal, but if it's on sale it's a no-brainer. Much respect for the game and the devs. Thank you for making this great and unique game. Keep up the good work!

review_text_raw:
A hacking turn-based tactical game.
  Its style is somewhat similar to hacking minigame in Deus Ex, but it is turn-based and significantly more complex. You have to navigate a grid of nodes, populated with ICE and sometimes hostile operators, while being traced by the system. There are many possible playstyles - from more cautious stealth oriented to quick, aggressive and dirty. These are also depending on loadout of your cyberdeck - both hardware and software. Managing limited number of actions in a turn, CPU slices for running programs and the system trace is the core of the strategy. And it is all exclusively controled by a very well implemented command line. The missions themselves are quite varied, sometimes even multi-phase, the special mention goes to the side quest styled as DnD dungeon adventure.
  On the strategic level you can choose missions and sometimes branch the story, participate in challenges and obtain programs and hardware to customize your deck. Some of the programs are useful only in a limited circumstances, while others are trusted universal tools. You are well advised to adapt your deck according to intel about the next mission. The story is quite interesting, heavy with cyberpunk and dystopian themes. Even side missions offer interesting look into the world. All of this is told using e-mails and text documents.
  The graphics and sound are clean and minimal, fitting with the setting. Sometimes music mixes in to support the change of atmosphere.
  It is a fresh concept and I recommend it for fans of cyberpunk and tactical/stealh games.

The game was pretty cool and I was glad I tried it out. 

+ The hacking style is neat and the story was engaging enough to follow it to its conclusion. The user interface can be confronting but as long as you're okay with a keyboard you should be able to pick it up. Because of the turn based nature (with real time as an additional option) you're never in danger of being too slow to select your next move and have plenty of time to plan and scope out the situation.

+ There's multiple tools that you can select in your hacking kit so you can approach the majority of puzzles/encounters with your own bit of flavour; only needing to swap out your kit for certain tools in certain situations. 

+ There was nice bit of choice in approaching a few quest lines with some even having follow ups depending on your decision. 

+ I love bonus objectives and things you can pursue beyond just the core story, finding and completing some 'secret' missions with worthwhile rewards at the end of them.

It only happened once on a long mission which felt upsetting but the rest of the game was decent enough to push through it. The other two times were fortunately on a short mission so it wasn't too bad to restart. [/strike] Should be fixed in an upcoming update :)

review_text_raw:
Wow, this was absolutely amazing. Yes, it is a bit hard to categorize -- it's more or less a Turn Based Strategy game with RPG elements and a strong story, completely immersed in the "hacking" theme. Do not expect a hacking sim, this is completely "gamefied", but that is exactly what makes it fun.

It starts a bit slow, but once you start to pick up upgrades, you start to think about the choices you must make (what software and hardware to pick for each assignment, for example). It isn't incredibly hard, but it will make you think if you want the best outcomes of all missions. And there are some "secret sidequests" which aren't too hard to find, just make sure you explore the game at your leisure.

But the good gameplay is there to support an amazing story; some of the story beats are really memorable, and expertly presented.

Now, do know the game is played with keyboard only (not even mouse). This is a stylistic choice which makes complete sense in the context of the game. And it **really** works, helping immensely with the illusion you are hacking something.

I run across very few bugs near the end of the game, but they were easily sidestepped. Very recommended, 92/100.

review_text_raw:
If you like [i]Hollywood Hacking[/i], you're going to love this one!

The hacking mechanic is turn-based, where you have to decide how to use your two action points, either by moving around the "network" you're hacking, or using a "program". Effectiveness of the programs depends on how many "slices" of power from your hardware you allocate to each one (re-allocating slices doesn't consume actions).

When your turn is done, your opponents (AIs, Sysops, other hackers...) will move following almost the same rules (for example, Sysadmins are not affected by the booby traps laid out in the network)

Your time on the network (the number of turns) is limited by a "Trace" that ends up aborting your mission.

Most of the story is conveyed by written email/chats. There are some moments that will require you to type an email or a chat message to progress. Those can be "hacker-typed" (quite fun, to be honest) or skipped by pressing TAB.

The background is a story about identity, revenge and AI. Very cool!

review_text_raw: I'm really fond of hacking and programming games. This one is one of the best. It's not realistic hacking by any measure—but it is hacking gamified in one of the best ways I know of. Basically, it's an RPG with turn-based tactical combat and a hackers-themed story with a great interface. The latter may be a point of contention for many — but I, personally, have great affinity for any developer who makes their game playable on keyboard alone (carpal tunnel syndrome is an issue for me). Here, keyboard is the only options, and you'll have to type commands or hotkeys for everything. To me, this adds a lot to the atmosphere and the feel of game. It's a Hollywood-esque take on "hacking" vibe-wise but at same time it's moderately deep from the perspective of tactics and deck-building. So, if something like Duskers and Hacknet is your thing, you're going to enjoy this game a lot. Grabbed during the sale for 5-6 bucks, it's a steal.

review_text_raw:
This game is very fun and *beautiful*.

It's a turn-based strategy with hand-crafted levels, and each new level is somehow interesting. The main story levels are the best but the even each new side level has a unique network composition or different hints or obstacles or even new gameplay elements, and together this makes it so that you're always looking forward to what you will see in the next level. The best experience is perhaps the level where you're chatting with your friend as you go, navigating a building and opening doors for her.

Another cool thing is that the game is beautiful. It has almost no art (some enemy defenses have pretty 3D models, but they're rare) but the interface shines. It has good fonts, crisp text rendering, sharp lines, no choppiness and is very responsive. Curiously, I find these things very important in text-based games and RPGs.
